paras: The lynching of Manna Ponton took place at Halifax, North Carolina, on the night of August 20–21, 1903, when a crowd hanged a young Black man accused of assaulting and murdering Mary Jenkins, a white girl, and riddled his body with bullets. He was taken from the citizens and officers holding him within hours of the discovery of the girl's body. White North Carolina editors defended the killing, and a committee of Black residents of Halifax condemned the crime while saying they did not encourage lynching.

Mary Jenkins, described as twelve or thirteen, was the granddaughter of a captain whom the Associated Press called Griffin and local papers called the late Capt. J. M. Grizzard. Ponton worked at the hotel and for the girl's family and lived with his sister.

On the evening of Thursday, August 20, the girl went to the stable near her home, reportedly to look for eggs, and did not return. Between seven and eight o'clock her body was found in the locked stable, tied in a bag, with the throat cut. Ponton was arrested when the stable keys were found in his pocket, and searchers reported a bloody knife and blood on his hands and clothes. He first said the blood came from cleaning fish, an account the Commonwealth said his sister contradicted.

While he was held "under guard of a large number of citizens, as well as deputies and constables," armed men came in from Weldon, and the Raleigh News and Observer predicted he would not "live to see daylight." Every account of a confession comes from those who held and killed him: the Associated Press said he confessed with the noose around his neck, the Commonwealth when the knife was produced. A crowd swelled by some seventy-five men from Weldon then took him, and a Weldon correspondent wrote that the officers "made a faint effort to protect their prisoner."

Ponton was hanged, from a tree limb according to the Associated Press or from a telegraph or telephone pole near the depot according to North Carolina reports, and shot; the Wilmington Messenger said "over 500 shots" were fired.

The body hung until two o'clock the next afternoon while hundreds came in to look at it, and was then buried at the county home. No report of an inquest, arrests or grand jury action appears in the coverage; the Weldon News called it Halifax county's first lynching.

A committee of Black residents, M. W. Williams, the Rev. A. J. Jackson and John H. Collins, sent resolutions to the Raleigh Post condemning "the negro and human brute Manna Ponton." They wrote that they did "not encourage lynching and would prefer the law to take its course," but that his fate "was not too severe."

The Associated Press carried the story nationally on August 21 under headlines such as "Hanged by a Mob" and "Hanged to a Tree," and condensed versions ran as far as Nevada and Rhode Island. These versions called Ponton only "a negro," stressed that the girl was white and repeated the confession as fact; a San Antonio brief called him a "colored rapist and throat cutter." Details drifted in retelling, and a Michigan brief called the girl "Mary Griffin" and said Ponton was "taken from jail."

North Carolina papers ran fuller accounts under headings such as "The Halifax Horror" and "Blackest Crime of the Age." Editors then defended the killing: the Concord Tribune said it was done "in the characteristic southern way, orderly, quietly," and the Weldon News wrote that the crime "is not a case for the courts." The Henderson Gold Leaf reprinted a "Southern Woman's" letter to the New York Herald that told the story without names and pleaded for "more lenient judgment" of lynchers.

The Gold Leaf and the Monroe Journal printed the Black residents' resolutions as a rare exception and used them to demand that Black leaders denounce crime rather than lynching. These resolutions, printed in white papers, are the only Black voices in the coverage.

The Commonwealth placed the hanging before midnight on August 20, the Weldon correspondent "early this morning" on August 21; the girl's age was thirteen in the wire report and twelve in local papers and the resolutions.

reader.title: Lynching of Manna Ponton
bases: A crowd seized Ponton from citizens and officers holding him after the girl's murder, hanged him and shot his body full of bullets (A3, A18, A29).

Ponton was hanged and shot by a crowd of hundreds, including some seventy-five men from Weldon, after officers made only 'a faint effort' to protect him (A18, A29); the killing punished an accused crime without trial, which white editors defended as punishment 'if not a strictly legal' and 'without judge or jury' (A32, A42).

The Associated Press report (A3), two independent Weldon correspondents (A18, A24), the Scotland Neck Commonwealth (A29) and the Halifax Black residents' resolutions (A39) all agree that a crowd hanged and shot Ponton at Halifax on the night after the girl's body was found.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: A crowd seized the suspect, who confessed with the noose around his neck, hanged him from a tree limb and riddled his body with bullets, then dispersed without concealment.

accounts.label: Weldon correspondents
accounts.gist: Ponton first said the blood was from cleaning fish, then confessed; officers made a faint effort to protect him before he was swung up to a telegraph (or telephone) pole and shot, reportedly over 500 times.

accounts.label: Scotland Neck Commonwealth (local)
accounts.gist: Ponton confessed when the knife was produced; before midnight he was hanging from a telegraph pole near the depot, where his body stayed until 2 p.m. the next day.

accounts.label: 'A Southern Woman' (letter to the New York Herald)
accounts.gist: An unnamed North Carolina town's hostler killed a 12-year-old girl in a stable and was identified by the key, the blood and his confession, and 'they hanged him within six hours of the crime.'

accounts.label: Halifax Black residents' committee
accounts.gist: Ponton was 'hanged and shot a few hours after' the crime; 'the right man was caught and made a confession'; they did not encourage lynching but called his fate not too severe.

framing.detail: Out-of-state papers ran the AP story under 'Hanged by a Mob', 'Hanged to a Tree', 'Paid the Penalty', calling Ponton only 'a negro' and treating the confession as fact.
North Carolina dailies headlined 'The Halifax Horror' and 'Blackest Crime of the Age', dwelling on the girl and calling Ponton a 'brute' and 'wretch'.
The Concord Tribune praised the lynching as done 'in the characteristic southern way, orderly, quietly'.
The Weldon News said the crime 'is not a case for the courts' and told Black preachers to denounce the crime, not the lynching.

The Raleigh Post, via the Washington Post, reprinted a 'Southern Woman's' plea for 'more lenient judgment' of lynchers, and the Gold Leaf and Monroe Journal printed the Black residents' resolutions as a rare exception while demanding more.
